Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old man with 4-day history of intensely itchy, sore, red skin affecting chest, hands and antecubital areas, interfering with sleep and work.
- Clinician impression: probable eczema flare; plan to prescribe a stronger topical steroid, emollients and consider antihistamine (follow-up in 1 week if not improved).

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Acute widespread pruritic, sore rash for 4 days, primarily chest, hands and inside elbows; described as red, very itchy, and sometimes cracked.
- Associated symptoms/negatives: severe itch disturbing sleep and concentration; no bleeding, no pus/discharge, no fever, no cough or breathing difficulties, no face involvement reported.
- Patient self-treated with an over-the-counter steroid cream purchased last night (name not documented) without relief; has tried antihistamines recently without benefit (type/dose not documented).
- Clinician observed the rash and documented it “appears quite familiar” consistent with eczema (examination details sparse).
- Clinical impression: likely eczema flare; differential not expanded in transcript.

Issue 2:
- Past history of eczema with prior response to prescription topical treatment.
- Past asthma in the past, reportedly resolved.
- No regular medications reported.

Issue 3:
- Functional impact: severe pruritus causing insomnia, impaired concentration at work, and limitation of recreational activity (unable to hike due to symptoms).
- No specialist/allied health review documented.

Medications:
- Over-the-counter steroid cream purchased last night — name/dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Antihistamines tried recently by patient — type/dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Clinician to prescribe a stronger topical steroid — name/dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Emollient for use in bath/shower prescribed/recommended — product/dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Clinician offered fexofenadine as prescription option — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Patient reports no regular medications.

Allergies:
- None reported.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema (history; prior episodes treated).
- Asthma in past (no longer active).

Social History:
- Age 31, lives with flatmates.
- Employed full-time as a project manager at a pharmaceutical company.
- Smoking: denies.
- Alcohol: occasional, a few beers per week.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care items (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, recent optometry or skin check) documented in transcript.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: none documented.
- Skin: patient reports dry, cracked areas; clinician states rash “appears quite familiar” and consistent with eczema based on visual assessment (no further lesion description provided).
- No discharge, bleeding, or systemic signs documented.

Plan:
- Prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid (specific agent and regimen not documented).
- Prescribe/recommend emollients for bath/shower use and regular moisturization; advise trial for 7–10 days before reassessing.
- Offer/consider oral antihistamine: clinician suggested fexofenadine (prescription) and discussed OTC options (loratadine or chlorpheniramine/Piriton) — patient previously tried antihistamines without benefit.
- Advise keeping a diary of possible triggers (soaps, shower gels, clothing) to identify exacerbating factors.
- Return/Follow-up: patient to re-present in one week if no improvement, or earlier if worsening.

document_quality / Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs, detailed skin examination findings (lesion morphology, extent), specific prescription names, doses, routes and frequencies for topical steroid, emollient and oral antihistamine; details of prior eczema treatments; exact name of OTC steroid cream used by patient.
- Internal conflicts: clinician initially stated intention to examine the rash then later said they had “looked at your skin” — possible minor conflict regarding whether a full examination was performed (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: audio/sound quality poor at times; occasional interruptions and inaudible segments noted.
